parts.sub: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy · c. 1450–1400 BC
Samuel, Saul, David, Solomon · c. 1060–930 BC
Kings, Chronicles and the prophets · 931–587 BC
Ezekiel, Daniel, Isaiah 40–66, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther · 597–430 BC
The four Gospels in one story · 6 BC – AD 30
John's letters and the Apocalypse · c. AD 95

stops.before: Nothing has happened yet. There is no world, only God — and the story begins by having him speak.
stops.watch: Count the sevens: seven days, seven 'and God saw that it was good'. Notice that man and woman are made last and made 'in our image', and that chapter 2 tells the making of Adam a second time, from the ground up, with a garden, a river and a rib.
stops.after: A garden, two trees, and one command not to eat.

stops.t: The serpent, the fruit and the gate
stops.before: Adam and Eve have everything, and one boundary. A talking serpent asks the first question in the Bible: 'Did God really say…?'
stops.watch: Read God's sentence on the serpent slowly — 'she shall crush thy head' in the Vulgate — because the whole rest of the book is the working out of that promise. Notice too that God makes them clothes before he sends them out.
stops.after: Outside the garden, the first brothers.

stops.before: East of Eden the first family farms and keeps sheep; two brothers bring two offerings, and only one is accepted.
stops.watch: The first murder, the first city, the first song — and the long list of names in chapter 5, each ending 'and he died', until Enoch, who 'walked with God, and was seen no more'.
stops.after: The earth fills with violence, and God decides to wash it clean.

stops.before: Ten generations from Adam, mankind has become so violent that God 'repents' of having made him. One man is found righteous.
stops.watch: The measurements of the ark (see the diagram), the raven and the dove, and the first covenant — sealed not by a promise from Noah but by a bow God hangs in the clouds against himself. Chapter 9 ends with a family scandal that shapes the map of nations.
stops.after: Noah's sons spread over the earth, and try to build their way back to heaven.

stops.before: From Noah's three sons come seventy nations — the 'table of nations' of chapter 10 is the Bible's first map of the world.
stops.watch: One language, one plan, one tower 'with its top in heaven' — and God coming down to look at something so small he has to stoop. The chapter ends with a genealogy that narrows from all nations to one family in Ur: Terah, and his son Abram.
stops.after: The story of everyone becomes the story of one man.

stops.before: A seventy-five-year-old man in Harran, childless, is told to leave everything for a land he has never seen, and promised that all nations will be blessed in him.
stops.watch: Three promises — land, descendants, blessing — that the rest of the Bible keeps returning to. Watch Abram's faith wobble in Egypt and stand firm with Lot; and meet Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem who brings out bread and wine.
stops.after: Ten years pass and there is still no child.

stops.before: Abram is old, Sarai is barren, and God has promised descendants. Abram suggests his servant could inherit; Sarai suggests her maid could bear the child.
stops.watch: 'He believed the Lord, and it was reputed to him unto justice' — Paul's favourite verse. The strange night-time covenant of the torch between the halves; Hagar, the first person in the Bible to name God; new names, Abraham and Sarah; and three visitors at the tent door, one of whom hears Sarah laugh.
stops.after: The visitors turn towards Sodom, and Abraham bargains for the city.

stops.before: Abraham has bargained God down to ten righteous men to spare Sodom. There are not ten.
stops.watch: Lot's hesitation, his wife's backward glance, and the cave. Then, after twenty-five years of waiting, a baby whose name means 'he laughs' — and Hagar and Ishmael sent into the desert, where God hears the boy crying.
stops.after: God has given the son. Now he asks for him back.

stops.before: Isaac is a boy, the only heir of every promise. God tells Abraham to take him to a mountain in the land of Moriah — the hill on which the Temple will one day stand.
stops.watch: 'God will provide himself the victim' — the son carrying the wood up the hill, and the ram caught in the thorns. Then the quiet chapters: Sarah's grave, the first piece of the promised land Abraham actually owns, and a servant finding a wife for Isaac at a well.
stops.after: Isaac and Rebecca have twins, and the younger is a schemer.

stops.before: Abraham dies. Isaac's twins, Esau and Jacob, have wrestled since the womb, and a bowl of stew has already changed hands.
stops.watch: Rebecca's plot, the goat skins, the blind father's blessing given to the wrong son — and Esau's terrible cry. Jacob flees, and on a stone pillow at Bethel dreams of a ladder with angels going up and down: the place where heaven touches earth.
stops.after: The trickster arrives at his uncle's house, and meets a better trickster.

stops.before: Twenty years with Laban: two wives instead of one, eleven sons, great flocks, and finally an escape. Ahead lies Esau with four hundred men.
stops.watch: The night by the Jabbok: Jacob alone, a stranger who wrestles until daybreak, a hip put out of joint, and a new name — Israel, 'he who strives with God'. Then the meeting with Esau, who runs to him and weeps.
stops.after: Israel settles in the land, and his favourite son is given a coat.

stops.before: Jacob has twelve sons, and loves one of them too openly. Joseph is seventeen, dreams of sheaves bowing to him, and tells his brothers.
stops.watch: The pit, the caravan, the coat dipped in blood. Then Egypt: Potiphar's wife, the prison, the butler's and baker's dreams, and Pharaoh's seven fat cows — and the slave becomes the second man in the kingdom. (Chapter 38, Judah and Tamar, seems an interruption; remember Tamar's name when you reach the first page of Matthew.)
stops.after: The famine comes, and the brothers who sold him come to Egypt to buy grain.

stops.before: Joseph rules Egypt's grain; his brothers, who think him long dead, stand before him and do not know him.
stops.watch: Joseph's tests — the silver cup, the demand for Benjamin — and Judah's speech offering himself in his brother's place, the longest speech in Genesis and the moment Joseph breaks. Then Jacob comes down to Egypt, and Israel is settled in Goshen.
stops.after: The old man blesses his sons, and Genesis closes with a coffin in Egypt.

stops.before: Jacob is dying in Egypt. He gathers his twelve sons — the twelve tribes — around his bed.
stops.watch: The crossed hands over Joseph's sons; the oracle on each tribe, above all Judah, from whom 'the sceptre shall not be taken away… till he come that is to be sent'. And Joseph's last word to his brothers: 'you thought evil against me, but God turned it into good.'
stops.after: Before Egypt turns against Israel, the story steps aside for one man's suffering.

stops.t: Job — why do the righteous suffer?
stops.before: Job lives outside Israel's story entirely, a wealthy and upright man in the land of Hus. Heaven has a wager on him.
stops.watch: Read the first three chapters and the last five, and as much of the friends' argument in between as you can bear — that is the point; they talk for thirty-four chapters and are wrong. Then God answers out of the whirlwind with questions, not answers: 'Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?'
stops.after: Back in Egypt, four centuries pass, and a new king arises who knew not Joseph.

stops.before: Joseph is forgotten. The Israelites have multiplied into a nation of slaves, and Pharaoh has ordered their baby boys drowned in the Nile.
stops.watch: Two midwives who fear God more than the king; a mother who hides her son three months, then sets him afloat; Pharaoh's daughter who names him 'drawn out'. Forty years later, a murder, a flight to Midian, a well and a wife — and God 'remembers his covenant'.
stops.after: At the back of the desert, a bush that burns and is not consumed.

stops.before: Moses is eighty, a shepherd for his father-in-law, far from Egypt and from any thought of his people.
stops.watch: 'Put off the shoes from thy feet.' God gives his name — the name so holy the Jews will not say it — and Moses gives five excuses, each answered. Aaron becomes his mouth. The first audience with Pharaoh goes badly: 'Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice?'
stops.after: Pharaoh has said no. God begins to take Egypt apart.

stops.before: Egypt is the greatest power on earth and its gods rule the river, the sun and the harvest. Each plague strikes one of them.
stops.watch: Blood, frogs, gnats, flies, cattle, boils, hail, locusts, darkness — and Pharaoh's heart, which he hardens and God hardens, alternately. Between each plague the tension is the same sentence: 'Let my people go.' The tenth is announced in chapter 11 and falls in the next stop.
stops.after: On the night of the tenth plague, the meal that Israel will eat for ever.

stops.before: Every house in Egypt will lose its firstborn tonight — unless its doorposts are marked with the blood of a lamb.
stops.watch: The lamb, the unleavened bread, the girded loins: the Passover, which is also the Last Supper's shape. The night flight, the pillar of cloud and fire, the sea standing up in walls, and Miriam's song on the far shore — the oldest poem in the Bible.
stops.after: Free, and in a desert with nothing to eat.

stops.before: Three days from the sea the water is bitter and the people already wish they had died in Egypt.
stops.watch: Manna — 'what is it?' — every morning except the Sabbath, and quail in the evening; water from the rock at Horeb; the first battle, won while Moses' arms are held up; and Jethro's advice that Moses cannot judge everyone alone. Watch the murmuring: it is the pattern of the next forty years.
stops.after: In the third month they come to the mountain, and God comes down.

stops.before: Israel camps at the foot of Sinai. God offers them something no nation has been offered: to be his own people, a kingdom of priests.
stops.watch: The Ten Words spoken out of fire and smoke while the people beg Moses to hear them instead; then the 'book of the covenant' — laws about slaves, oxen, widows and strangers — and the blood sprinkled on the people. Chapter 24 ends with seventy elders eating and drinking in the sight of God.
stops.after: Moses goes up the mountain for forty days to receive the plan of a tent.

stops.before: God will travel with his people. He describes, cubit by cubit, the tent he will live in, and the clothes his priest will wear.
stops.watch: Read with the diagrams open: the Ark and the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, the curtains, the altar — everything moving inward toward one room. Chapter 28 dresses Aaron: the twelve stones over his heart and 'Holy to the Lord' on his forehead.
stops.after: While Moses is still on the mountain, the people below make a god they can see.

stops.before: Forty days is too long. The people ask Aaron for gods to go before them, and he makes one from their earrings.
stops.watch: Moses arguing God out of destroying Israel, then smashing the tablets himself; the Levites' terrible zeal; and the greatest conversation in the Old Testament — 'Show me thy glory' — answered by God passing by and naming himself 'merciful and gracious, patient and of much compassion'. Moses comes down with his face shining.
stops.after: Forgiven, the people build the tent exactly as it was shown.

stops.before: The people who gave gold for a calf now give so much for the Tabernacle that Moses has to tell them to stop.
stops.watch: Bezalel and Oholiab, the first artists filled with the Spirit of God. Then, on the first day of the first month of the second year, the tent goes up and the cloud comes down — and Moses himself cannot enter. Exodus ends with God living in the middle of the camp.
stops.after: A God this close needs rules for approaching him: Leviticus.

stops.before: The tent is built and the priests are ready. Leviticus is the manual — and the book where most readers give up. Take the doors that open onto the story.
stops.watch: Chapter 1 shows what a sacrifice was; 8–10 ordain Aaron, and two of his sons die for offering 'strange fire'; 16 is the Day of Atonement, the one day the high priest passes the veil; 19 holds 'thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'. The rest is there when you want it.
stops.after: The camp is counted, ordered, and set marching.

stops.t: Grapes of Canaan, forty years of sand
stops.before: Eleven days from Sinai to the edge of the promised land. Twelve spies go in and come back with a cluster of grapes so big two men carry it — and with fear.
stops.watch: The people refuse to go up, and God turns them round for forty years until that generation dies. Korah's rebellion and the earth opening; Aaron's rod that buds; Moses striking the rock in anger and losing the land himself; the bronze serpent on a pole that Jesus will compare himself to.
stops.after: On the plains of Moab a pagan prophet is hired to curse Israel.

stops.before: Israel is camped across the Jordan from Jericho, and the king of Moab is terrified.
stops.watch: The prophet who cannot say what he is paid to say, the donkey who sees the angel first, and the oracle that looks past Moab's day: 'A star shall rise out of Jacob.' In chapter 27 Moses climbs a mountain to see the land, and lays hands on Joshua.
stops.after: Moses, a hundred and twenty years old, turns to the people for three last speeches.

stops.before: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell: the whole story retold to the children of those who left Egypt, on the last day of his life.
stops.watch: The Ten Commandments again, then the sentence every Jew still prays twice a day: 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart' — the verse Jesus calls the greatest commandment. And the warning: when you are full, do not forget.
stops.after: Blessings, curses, a song, and a grave no one has found.

stops.before: The covenant is renewed with blessings and curses laid out like two roads. Moses has one mountain left to climb.
stops.watch: 'I have set before you life and death… choose therefore life.' The song of Moses, the blessing of the tribes, and then Nebo: God shows him the whole land and buries him himself. 'There arose no more a prophet in Israel like unto Moses' — until, the Gospels will say, one greater.
stops.after: Joshua stands at the Jordan with the promise in his hands.

stops.t: Be strong and of good courage
stops.before: Moses is dead. Joshua, his aide since Sinai, must lead a nation of ex-nomads across a river in flood against walled cities.
stops.watch: God's charge to Joshua, three times: be strong. The two spies and Rahab the harlot, who hides them and hangs a scarlet cord in her window — she will turn up in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The Jordan stops flowing as the Ark enters it, and twelve stones are set up on the far bank.
stops.after: The first city stands in the way.

stops.before: Israel is inside Canaan, circumcised, and eating Passover with the manna stopped — the land's own grain for the first time.
stops.watch: A commander of the Lord's army with a drawn sword; seven days of marching and trumpets; the walls fall flat. Then defeat at Ai because one man, Achan, kept what was under the ban — and the whole people are held responsible.
stops.after: The conquest is told in campaigns, then the land is shared out.

stops.t: The sun stands still; the land divided
stops.before: The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty with mouldy bread; five kings attack them for it, and Israel must keep its word.
stops.watch: The long day at Gibeon. Then chapters 13–21 divide the land tribe by tribe — read them with the map of the tribes open rather than verse by verse — and Joshua's farewell at Shechem: 'Choose this day whom you will serve; as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.'
stops.after: Joshua dies, and the generation that knew him dies — and then 'there arose another generation that knew not the Lord'.

stops.t: Every man did what was right in his own eyes
stops.before: Without Joshua the tribes drift apart, worship the local gods, and are overrun — then cry out, and God raises a deliverer. Judges turns this circle a dozen times, and each turn is darker.
stops.watch: Chapter 2 gives the pattern. Then Ehud the left-handed, Deborah the prophetess under her palm tree and Jael with her tent-peg, and Gideon, threshing wheat in a winepress to hide from the Midianites, whose army God cuts from 32,000 to 300 so that no one can boast.
stops.after: The last and strongest of the judges is also the least wise.

stops.before: The Philistines, sea-people settled on the coast, now rule Israel. A childless couple in Dan is promised a son who must never cut his hair.
stops.watch: The lion, the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone — and the man who could kill a thousand undone by a woman who asked three times. Blind in Gaza, grinding at the mill, he prays once. Chapters 17–21 that follow are the book's grim coda: no king, and everyone doing what was right in his own eyes.
stops.after: In the same dark age, a small story of loyalty in a Bethlehem barley field.

stops.before: A famine drives a family from Bethlehem to Moab; the men die; the widow Naomi goes home with nothing but a foreign daughter-in-law who refuses to leave her.
stops.watch: Ruth's vow, the gleaning, the threshing floor at midnight, the sandal at the gate. And the last four verses, a genealogy: Ruth the Moabite is David's great-grandmother — and so an ancestor of Jesus.
stops.after: Israel is about to ask for a king. First it needs a prophet.

stops.before: Hannah weeps for a child in the shrine at Shiloh, is taken for a drunk by the priest, and promises the boy to God before he is born.
stops.watch: Hannah's song (Mary will echo it), the boy hearing his name in the night, the Ark captured by the Philistines and returned on a cart pulled by cows. Then the elders come to old Samuel: 'Give us a king, as all nations have' — and God says, they have not rejected you, they have rejected me.
stops.after: Samuel is sent to anoint a tall young man looking for his father's donkeys.

stops.t: Saul, the king who could not wait
stops.before: Israel gets its king: head and shoulders taller than anyone, modest at first, victorious against the Ammonites.
stops.watch: Two failures that end him: offering the sacrifice himself rather than wait for Samuel, and sparing the Amalekite king and the best sheep. 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' Samuel turns to go, Saul tears his cloak, and the kingdom is torn with it.
stops.after: Samuel goes to Bethlehem with a horn of oil, and a shepherd boy is fetched from the field.

stops.before: 'Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart.' The youngest of eight is anointed in secret, and taken to court to play the harp for the king's black moods.
stops.watch: The giant's armour itemised piece by piece, and the boy who refuses Saul's; five smooth stones; 'the Lord saveth not with sword and spear'. Then Jonathan's love for David, and Saul's jealousy beginning with a song: 'Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands.'
stops.after: The king who anointed him now wants him dead, and David runs.

stops.before: David is a fugitive with six hundred men in the caves of the Judean desert, and Saul hunts him with the army.
stops.watch: Jonathan's arrows and the farewell at the stone; twice David has Saul in his hands, in the cave and in the sleeping camp, and twice will not touch 'the Lord's anointed'. Saul, abandoned by God, consults a witch at Endor and meets the ghost of Samuel. He dies on Mount Gilboa, and Jonathan with him.
stops.after: David's grief is a poem, and then he is king — of Judah only.

stops.before: Seven years of civil war between David in Hebron and Saul's house. Then the tribes come to Hebron and make him king of all Israel.
stops.watch: 'How are the valiant fallen' — David's lament over Saul and Jonathan. The capture of Jerusalem, a neutral city between the tribes, up the water shaft; the Ark brought in with David dancing before it; and chapter 7, the promise that his throne will stand for ever — the root of every hope for a Messiah.
stops.after: At the height of his power, one spring evening on the roof.

stops.before: The army is at war and the king has stayed home. From his roof he sees a woman bathing.
stops.watch: Adultery, then a letter that sends her husband to his death carried by the man himself. Nathan's parable of the one ewe lamb, and the king who condemns himself. David's repentance is Psalm 50 (51 in Hebrew numbering), the Miserere: 'Create a clean heart in me, O God.' The child dies; Solomon is born.
stops.after: 'The sword shall never depart from thy house.' It begins with his own sons.

stops.before: David's eldest son rapes his half-sister Tamar; her brother Absalom kills him for it, flees, returns, and begins to steal the hearts of Israel.
stops.watch: David walking barefoot up the Mount of Olives, weeping, as his son takes his city — the route Jesus will take on another night; the mule, the oak, Absalom hanging by his hair; and the king's cry when they bring the news he asked for.
stops.after: David is old and cold, and two sons want the throne.

stops.before: Before leaving David, sit with the prayers the Bible puts in his mouth — the psalms were sung in his Temple and are still prayed every hour of every day.
stops.watch: Psalm 1, the two ways; 8, the heavens and the son of man; 18 (19), the heavens tell the glory; 21 (22), 'My God, why hast thou forsaken me', prayed on the cross; 22 (23), the shepherd; 26 (27), the Lord is my light; 41 (42), the deer at the stream; 62 (63), thirsting in the desert. The Vulgate numbers run one behind the Hebrew from 10 to 147.
stops.after: David's last act is to name his heir.

stops.t: Give thy servant an understanding heart
stops.before: Adonijah proclaims himself king while David lies dying; Nathan and Bathsheba move fast, and Solomon is anointed at Gihon.
stops.watch: David's last charge, with old scores settled. Then Solomon's dream at Gibeon — offered anything, he asks for wisdom — and the two mothers and one living child: the judgment the whole world remembers.
stops.after: The wise king builds what his father was not allowed to.

stops.before: Cedar from Lebanon, stone dressed at the quarry, 180,000 labourers, seven years. Read chapter 6 with the diagram of the Temple beside it.
stops.watch: The Ark carried in and the cloud filling the house so the priests cannot stand; Solomon's prayer of dedication — 'will God indeed dwell upon earth? the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee' — and the thought that foreigners too will come to pray here.
stops.after: Solomon's wisdom draws the world to Jerusalem, and his wives draw him away.

stops.before: The queen of Sheba comes to test him; gold arrives by the ton; and the tradition gathers three books under his name.
stops.watch: Proverbs 1–3, the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom, and Lady Wisdom calling in the streets; Ecclesiastes' 'vanity of vanities' and its time for everything; the Song of Songs, a love poem the Church reads as Christ and his bride. Then 1 Kings 11: seven hundred wives, other gods, and the sentence — the kingdom will be torn from your son.
stops.after: Solomon dies, and at his son's coronation the north walks out.

stops.before: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be crowned, and the tribes ask him to lighten his father's yoke. He asks the old men, then the young men, and listens to the young.
stops.watch: 'My little finger is thicker than my father's loins.' Ten tribes go with Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so his people will not go south to the Temple — the sin every northern king after him is measured by. See the diagram of the two kingdoms; from here the story runs on two tracks.
stops.after: Fifty years and a dozen kings on, the north gets its Ahab, and God sends a man from Gilead.

stops.before: Ahab has married Jezebel of Tyre and built Baal a temple in Samaria. A prophet in a hair cloak announces there will be no rain until he says so.
stops.watch: The widow's flour that does not run out; the contest on Carmel — 'Cry louder, perhaps your god is asleep' — and fire from heaven; then Elijah running from one woman's threat to Horeb, where God is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. Read chapter 21, Naboth's vineyard, for what Ahab and Jezebel were.
stops.after: Elijah goes up in a whirlwind, and his cloak falls to Elisha.

stops.before: 'Where is the Lord God of Elijah?' — Elisha strikes the Jordan with the cloak and it parts.
stops.watch: The Shunammite's son raised, the oil that fills every jar, Naaman the Syrian general told to bathe in the muddy Jordan and cured of leprosy, the axe-head that floats, the horses of fire around Dothan. Then Jehu's bloody coup: Jezebel thrown from her window, and Baal's temple made a latrine.
stops.after: A prophet is sent to the enemy capital, and runs the other way.

stops.before: Assyria is the terror of the age and Nineveh its capital. God tells Jonah to go and preach there; he buys a ticket to the opposite end of the sea.
stops.watch: Four short chapters, funny and sharp: the storm, the lot, the great fish and the psalm from its belly; a city that repents in sackcloth down to the cattle; and a prophet sulking under a gourd because God was merciful. Jesus will call his own death and resurrection 'the sign of Jonah'.
stops.after: Two more prophets go north, and they are not gentle.

stops.before: Under Jeroboam II the north is rich, religious and rotten. A shepherd from Tekoa in Judah walks into the royal shrine at Bethel.
stops.watch: Amos: 'for three crimes, and for four' round the neighbours until the finger lands on Israel; the plumb line; 'I hate and reject your festivals'. Hosea, told to marry a prostitute and take her back, so that Israel can see what God's love for an unfaithful people looks like: 'I will not execute the fierceness of my wrath… for I am God and not man.'
stops.after: In the south, in the year King Uzziah dies, a young man sees the Lord.

stops.before: Isaiah is a Jerusalem aristocrat and the greatest poet in the Bible; his book will end up quoted in the New Testament more than any other.
stops.watch: The seraphim, the coal on his lips, 'Here am I, send me'. The sign to a frightened king: a virgin shall conceive, Emmanuel. 'The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light… a child is born to us'; the shoot from the root of Jesse, and the wolf lying down with the lamb. Micah, his contemporary, names Bethlehem.
stops.after: The north falls first.

stops.before: Assyria has been squeezing Israel for a generation. Hoshea, the last king, stops paying tribute and writes to Egypt.
stops.watch: Three years of siege, Samaria taken, the people deported across the empire and never heard of again. Chapter 17 is the historian's verdict — the reasons, listed — and then foreigners settled in the empty land: the Samaritans of the Gospels.
stops.after: Twenty years later the same army stands under the walls of Jerusalem.

stops.before: Hezekiah has smashed the idols, dug a tunnel to bring the spring inside the walls, and refused Assyria's tribute. Sennacherib's field commander shouts terms up at the wall in Hebrew.
stops.watch: The letter Hezekiah spreads out before the Lord in the Temple; Isaiah's answer; and the angel who strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp in a night — Sennacherib's own annals admit he never took the city. Then the king's illness, the sundial that goes back, and the envoys from Babylon shown all the treasure.
stops.after: Hezekiah's son undoes everything, for fifty-five years.

stops.t: The book found in the Temple
stops.before: Manasseh has put altars to the stars inside the Temple and burned his own son. His grandson Josiah becomes king at eight.
stops.watch: Workmen repairing the Temple find a scroll of the Law; the king tears his clothes when it is read. The greatest reform in Judah's history: Passover kept as it had not been since the Judges. Nahum sings over the fall of Nineveh in 612; Habakkuk asks why the wicked prosper and is told 'the just shall live in his faith'. And Josiah dies at Megiddo — Armageddon.
stops.after: The last prophet of the kingdom has been preaching since Josiah's day, and nobody wants to hear him.

stops.t: Jeremiah — a fire in my bones
stops.before: Called as a boy — 'I know not how to speak, for I am a child' — Jeremiah must tell his city for forty years that Babylon will win and that resisting is fighting God.
stops.watch: The almond rod and the boiling pot; the Temple sermon ('the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord'); the potter's house; the yoke; the scroll the king cuts up and burns column by column; the cistern. And in the middle of the ruin, chapter 31: a new covenant, written on hearts.
stops.after: The first deportation takes the king and the craftsmen; among the exiles is a young priest named Ezekiel.

stops.before: Zedekiah, the last king, breaks his oath to Nebuchadnezzar. The siege lasts eighteen months; mothers eat their children.
stops.watch: The wall breached, the king caught near Jericho, his sons killed before his eyes and then the eyes put out; the Temple burned in the fifth month, the bronze pillars broken up and carried away. Lamentations is the city's own voice in the ashes, five alphabet-poems — and in the middle of the third, 'the mercies of the Lord are not ended; they are new every morning.'
stops.after: By the rivers of Babylon.

stops.before: The exiles are settled by the canals of Babylon, the greatest city in the world, with its blue gate and its ziggurat — Babel again.
stops.watch: Psalm 136 (137): the harps on the willows, 'if I forget thee, O Jerusalem', and the terrible last verse. The psalms of Asaph and the sons of Korah around it are the people arguing with God about what has happened, and Psalm 89 (90), 'Lord, thou hast been our refuge', is Moses' answer.
stops.after: On the banks of the Chebar canal a priest sees the heavens opened.

stops.t: The wheels and the dry bones
stops.before: Ezekiel was taken in the first deportation, ten years before the Temple fell. He is a priest with no temple, a prophet among people who think the worst is over.
stops.watch: The chariot of living creatures and wheels within wheels; the scroll he must eat; the glory of God leaving the Temple by the east gate in chapter 10. Then, after the fall, hope: the shepherd who will search for his sheep; a heart of flesh for a heart of stone; and the valley of dry bones — 'Son of man, can these bones live?'
stops.after: Meanwhile at Nebuchadnezzar's court, four Jewish boys refuse the king's food.

stops.t: The furnace and the lions' den
stops.before: Daniel and his three friends are trained for the Babylonian civil service and rise in it without ever bowing to its gods.
stops.watch: The statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, and the stone cut without hands; three men walking in the furnace with a fourth 'like the Son of God' (the Song of the Three, verses 24–90, is sung there); the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast; the lions. Chapters 13–14, Susanna and Bel, are Daniel the detective.
stops.after: In exile a second voice takes up Isaiah's scroll, and it sings.

stops.t: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people
stops.before: Isaiah 40 opens a new book within the book: the exile is nearly over, and a shepherd-king from Persia is on the horizon.
stops.watch: 'Every valley shall be exalted'; 'they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength'; the four Servant songs, above all chapter 53 — 'he was wounded for our iniquities… like a sheep to the slaughter' — the chapter the Ethiopian was reading when Philip met him. 'Come, all you that thirst.'
stops.after: In one night Babylon falls to Cyrus, exactly as Isaiah had named him.

stops.before: Cyrus of Persia, having taken Babylon, sends the peoples home to rebuild their temples — Jews included, with the vessels Nebuchadnezzar looted.
stops.watch: Forty-two thousand go up; the altar first, then foundations laid to trumpets while the old men who remembered Solomon's Temple weep. Opposition stops the work for sixteen years, until Haggai shames them — 'you live in panelled houses while this house lies waste' — and Zechariah sees the visions of the night. Dedicated 515 BC.
stops.after: Far away in Susa, a Jewish orphan girl becomes queen of Persia.

stops.t: For such a time as this
stops.before: Xerxes has dismissed his queen for refusing to appear at a banquet, and holds a beauty contest for a new one. Esther hides that she is a Jew.
stops.watch: Haman's plot to kill every Jew in the empire, decided by lot (pur); Mordecai's word to Esther — 'who knoweth whether thou art not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?'; three days' fast; the king's sleepless night; Haman hanged on his own gallows. God is never named, and everywhere. Chapters 11–16 in the Vulgate are the Greek additions, including Esther's prayer.
stops.after: Two books of the same age tell of deliverance in other courts: Judith and Tobit.

stops.before: Two stories the Vulgate keeps and the Hebrew Bible does not. Tobit: a blind exile in Nineveh, his son on a journey with a stranger who is more than he seems, and a fish. Judith: a widow and a general's tent.
stops.watch: Raphael revealing himself — 'I am one of the seven who stand before the Lord'; Tobias and Sarah's wedding prayer, read at Catholic weddings still. Judith's prayer, her beauty, the head of Holofernes in a bag, and her song.
stops.after: Back in Jerusalem the walls are still rubble, and a cupbearer in Susa hears of it.

stops.before: Ezra the scribe has come up with the Law in his hand; Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, weeps at the news of the broken walls and asks leave to go.
stops.watch: The night ride round the ruins; fifty-two days of building with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other; the wall finished 'and the enemies perceived that this work was wrought by God'. Then chapter 8: Ezra on a wooden platform reading the Law from morning to midday, the people weeping, and told instead to feast. Malachi closes the prophets with a promise to send Elijah.
stops.after: The Old Testament's story goes quiet for three hundred years — but not its wisdom, and not its wars.

stops.before: Alexander has conquered the world and Greek is its language. Jews in Jerusalem and Alexandria write wisdom for a people who now argue with philosophers.
stops.watch: Sirach's grandson translated his grandfather's book: practical wisdom on friends, money, daughters and doctors, and chapter 24, Wisdom speaking of herself as the Law. The Book of Wisdom, in Greek from Alexandria: the souls of the just 'are in the hand of God', and the righteous man whom the wicked plot to kill — a page the Passion narrative echoes.
stops.after: A Greek king decides the Jews will be Greeks too.

stops.before: Antiochus IV Epiphanes forbids circumcision and Sabbath, and sacrifices a pig on the altar of the Temple — 'the abomination of desolation'.
stops.watch: An old priest in Modein kills the king's officer and the collaborator at the altar, and his five sons take to the hills; Judas 'the Hammer' wins battle after battle; the Temple cleansed and rededicated — Hanukkah. 2 Maccabees 7: the mother and her seven sons, the first clear statement of the resurrection of the body. Daniel 7–12, the visions, belong to these years.
stops.after: The Maccabees' heirs quarrel, Rome is invited in, and Pompey walks into the Holy of Holies. Sixty years later, in a client king's reign, Gabriel is sent to a village in Galilee.

stops.t: In the beginning was the Word
stops.d: before all time — and c. 6 BC
stops.before: Four hundred years after Malachi. Rome rules; Herod, an Idumean, is king by Rome's favour; the Temple he is rebuilding is the wonder of the East. The story begins three times.
stops.watch: John begins before Genesis: the Word who was God became flesh. Matthew begins with a family tree — count the women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — and Joseph's dream. Luke begins in the Temple with an old priest struck dumb, and an angel in Nazareth: 'Hail, full of grace' — and Mary's yes. Her song, the Magnificat, is Hannah's song reborn.
stops.after: A census, a journey south, and no room at the inn.

stops.before: Micah named the town seven centuries ago. Caesar's decree brings a carpenter and his pregnant wife to it.
stops.watch: The manger, the shepherds, the angels' Gloria; Simeon in the Temple, who has waited his whole life for this and now can die — 'a sign that shall be contradicted, and thy own soul a sword shall pierce'. Then Matthew: the magi and the star, Herod's fury, the flight into Egypt and the slaughter of the innocents. And the boy of twelve, lost for three days, found in his Father's house.
stops.after: Thirty silent years in Nazareth. Then a voice in the desert.

stops.before: John, Zechariah's son, is in the Jordan valley in camel hair, eating locusts, baptising crowds and calling the Pharisees a brood of vipers. The Elijah Malachi promised.
stops.watch: Jesus comes to be baptised — and heaven opens, the Spirit descends, a voice: 'This is my beloved Son.' Then forty days in the desert and three temptations, each answered from Deuteronomy. Luke's genealogy runs back not to Abraham but to Adam.
stops.after: John points, and two of his disciples follow the Lamb of God.

stops.before: John's Gospel tells the first year, before the others begin: a week of callings, and a wedding.
stops.watch: Andrew, Peter, Philip, Nathanael under the fig tree. Water into wine at Cana, the first sign, at his mother's word. The whip in the Temple. Nicodemus by night — 'unless a man be born again' and 'God so loved the world'. The Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, the longest conversation Jesus has with anyone in the Gospels.
stops.after: John is arrested. Jesus goes north to Galilee, and the kingdom is announced.

stops.t: The kingdom of God is at hand
stops.before: Nazareth rejects him — a prophet is not without honour except in his own country — and Capernaum, on the lake, becomes his town.
stops.watch: Mark's breathless first chapters: fishermen called from their nets, a demon shouting his name in the synagogue, Peter's mother-in-law, a leper, a paralytic lowered through the roof — 'thy sins are forgiven thee' — Levi the tax collector at his table, the twelve chosen on a mountain. Watch how quickly the scribes decide he must die.
stops.after: On a hillside above the lake, he sits down to teach.

stops.before: The new Moses goes up a mountain, but instead of receiving a law he gives one.
stops.watch: The Beatitudes; salt and light; 'you have heard it said… but I say to you'; love your enemies; the Our Father; the lilies of the field; the narrow gate; the house on rock. Three chapters that the world, believing or not, has never been able to put down.
stops.after: Words, then works — a day of miracles by the sea.

stops.before: The crowds are so thick he teaches from a boat. He speaks only in parables now — the sower, the seed growing secretly, the mustard seed.
stops.watch: The storm on the lake, and the question that hangs over the whole Gospel: 'Who is this, that both wind and sea obey him?' The Gerasene demoniac and the pigs; Jairus's daughter and the woman who touched his cloak; the Baptist's head on a dish; five loaves and two fish for five thousand; and Jesus walking on the water.
stops.after: After the bread, a hard saying, and many walk away.

stops.t: I am the bread of life
stops.before: The crowd he fed wants to make him king. In the synagogue at Capernaum he tells them what the bread means.
stops.watch: 'Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood…' — and 'Will you also go away?' Peter: 'Lord, to whom shall we go?' Mark 7–8: what defiles a man, the Syrophoenician woman's crumbs, the deaf man, and at Caesarea Philippi the confession — 'Thou art the Christ' — followed at once by the first prediction of the cross, and Peter rebuked.
stops.after: Six days later, on a high mountain, three of them see him as he is.

stops.before: Peter, James and John go up the mountain with him and he begins to pray.
stops.watch: His face shining like the sun, Moses and Elijah — the Law and the Prophets — talking with him about his 'departure' at Jerusalem, the cloud, the voice. Then straight down into a crowd and a boy no one could heal: 'I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.' Matthew 18: the child in the midst, the lost sheep, seventy times seven.
stops.after: He sets his face toward Jerusalem, and Luke gives him a long road to teach on.

stops.before: Luke's 'travel narrative' — ten chapters on the way south, full of the parables only he records.
stops.watch: The seventy-two sent out; the Good Samaritan; Martha and Mary; the rich fool; the narrow door; the great supper; the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son — the Prodigal, the finest short story ever told; the dishonest steward; Lazarus and the rich man; the Pharisee and the publican.
stops.after: In Jerusalem for the feasts, John shows the quarrel sharpening.

stops.before: At Tabernacles and at the Dedication, in Herod's Temple, Jesus speaks in the open and the authorities try to arrest him.
stops.watch: The woman taken in adultery and the finger writing in the dust; 'I am the light of the world'; the man born blind, whose parents are afraid and who ends up seeing more than the Pharisees; the good shepherd who lays down his life; and the claim that makes them pick up stones: 'Before Abraham was made, I AM.'
stops.after: A message comes from Bethany: the one you love is sick.

stops.before: Jesus waits two days, then goes to a tomb four days sealed. Martha meets him on the road: 'If thou hadst been here…'
stops.watch: 'I am the resurrection and the life.' Jesus wept. The stone, the cry, the man bound in grave-clothes. From that day the council decides he must die — 'it is expedient that one man should die for the people'. Mary anoints his feet; Zacchaeus climbs his tree in Jericho; and on Sunday, the colt and the palms.
stops.after: Holy Week. Every hour of it is written down.

stops.t: The Temple, the fig tree, the widow's coins
stops.before: Jesus enters the city as the prophets said the king would, on a donkey, and goes straight to the Temple. Read with the diagram of Herod's Temple open.
stops.watch: The tables overturned in the Court of the Gentiles; the fig tree; the wicked tenants — told to the priests' faces; the coin with Caesar's head; the widow's two mites in the treasury; and, on the Mount of Olives, the prophecy that not one stone will be left, the abomination of desolation, the Son of man coming on the clouds. Matthew adds the ten virgins, the talents, the sheep and the goats.
stops.after: Thursday evening. An upper room, a basin, a loaf and a cup.

stops.before: Judas has already gone to the priests. Jesus sends two disciples after a man carrying a water jar to find the room.
stops.watch: 'This is my body… this is the chalice of my blood' — the Passover become the Eucharist. In John, no bread and wine but the washing of feet, the new commandment, 'I am the way', the vine and the branches, the promise of the Paraclete, and the long prayer of chapter 17: 'that they may be one.' Then out, across the Kidron, to a garden.
stops.after: Gethsemane, the kiss, the trial, the cock-crow, the cross.

stops.before: Follow the map: the garden, the high priest's house, the praetorium, Golgotha — a few hundred paces each, between nine at night and three in the afternoon.
stops.watch: 'Not what I will, but what thou wilt.' Peter's three denials; 'Are you the king of the Jews?'; Barabbas; the scourging and the crown; Ecce homo; Simon of Cyrene; the seven last words across the four Gospels — 'Father, forgive them', 'this day thou shalt be with me in paradise', 'Woman, behold thy son', 'why hast thou forsaken me', 'I thirst', 'It is consummated', 'into thy hands'. The veil torn; the centurion; Joseph's new tomb.
stops.after: The Sabbath. Then, before dawn on the first day of the week, women with spices.

stops.before: The stone is rolled away and the tomb is empty. Each Gospel tells the morning differently, and all four agree on that.
stops.watch: Mary Magdalene and the gardener — 'Mary.' Peter and John running; the road to Emmaus and the breaking of bread; Thomas's hand in the wound; breakfast on the beach and 'Simon, son of John, lovest thou me?' three times, for three denials; 'Go, teach all nations… I am with you all days.' And the Ascension from the Mount of Olives.
stops.after: Ten days later, a sound like a mighty wind.

stops.before: A hundred and twenty people in an upper room, praying, with Mary among them. It is the feast of the giving of the Law on Sinai.
stops.watch: Tongues of fire; Peter, who hid from a servant girl seven weeks ago, preaching to thousands — and three thousand baptised; the believers holding all things in common; the lame man at the Beautiful Gate: 'Silver and gold I have none.' The Sanhedrin cannot stop them: 'we cannot but speak.'
stops.after: The first martyr, and the persecution that spreads the Gospel by scattering it.

stops.before: Ananias and Sapphira have died for a lie; seven deacons are chosen to serve tables, and one of them cannot stop preaching.
stops.watch: Stephen's speech, the whole Old Testament retold as a story of a stiff-necked people, ending 'I see the heavens opened'; the stones; the young man minding the coats, named Saul. Then Philip in Samaria, and the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot.
stops.after: Saul, breathing threats, takes the road to Damascus.

stops.before: The Church's most dangerous enemy is thrown to the ground by a light and a voice.
stops.watch: Three days blind; Ananias's fear; the basket down the wall. Peter's vision of the sheet of unclean animals and Cornelius the centurion — the door opened to the Gentiles. Antioch, where they are first called Christians; James killed; Peter freed by an angel while the church prays, and the girl who leaves him standing at the gate.
stops.after: The church at Antioch lays hands on Barnabas and Saul and sends them west.

stops.before: Cyprus, Galatia, then — after a vision of a man of Macedonia — Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth.
stops.watch: The Council of Jerusalem in chapter 15, which decides that Gentiles need not become Jews — the hinge of the book. Paul and Silas singing in the Philippian jail; the Areopagus speech to the philosophers ('to the unknown God'); Corinth, where he stays eighteen months. Galatians and the Thessalonian letters are written on these roads: 'it is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me.'
stops.after: Three years in Ephesus, and letters to a church that is tearing itself apart.

stops.before: From Ephesus, where the silversmiths riot for Diana, Paul writes to the Corinthians about factions, lawsuits, immorality, the Eucharist, and a resurrection some of them doubt.
stops.watch: 'The word of the cross is foolishness to them that perish'; the Lord's Supper as he received it; the body and its members; the hymn to charity (13); and chapter 15, 'if Christ be not risen, your faith is vain'. Then Romans, his summa, written from Corinth: all have sinned; justified by faith; nothing can separate us from the love of God (8).
stops.after: He goes up to Jerusalem knowing what waits there.

stops.before: Arrested in the Temple on a false charge, rescued by Roman soldiers from a lynch mob, Paul appeals to Caesar.
stops.watch: His defence on the fortress steps; the plot of forty men; two years in Caesarea; the shipwreck on Malta, told by Luke who was aboard; and Rome, under house arrest, 'preaching the kingdom with all confidence, without prohibition'. From that house: Philippians' hymn — 'he emptied himself' — and Ephesians on the Church as his body and bride.
stops.after: Last letters, from Paul and from Peter, as Nero's fire lights the city.

stops.t: I have fought the good fight
stops.before: Paul writes to Timothy from his last prison; Peter writes to the churches of Asia as 'a witness of the sufferings of Christ'. Both die under Nero.
stops.watch: 'I have finished my course, I have kept the faith'; Peter's 'a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood'; James's faith without works is dead, and the tongue as a fire; Hebrews' roll-call of faith (11) and 'a cloud of witnesses'. The pastoral letters build the church that will outlive the apostles: bishops, deacons, widows, sound doctrine.
stops.after: Jerusalem falls to Titus in 70, as Jesus said. One apostle remains, very old, on an island.

stops.before: The last of the twelve, at Ephesus, writes to churches troubled by teachers who say Christ only seemed to have a body.
stops.watch: 'That which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled'; walking in the light; 'little children, love one another'; 'God is love, and he that abideth in love abideth in God.' Short, plain, and the whole Gospel.
stops.after: On the Lord's day, on Patmos, a voice like a trumpet.

stops.before: Exiled 'for the word of God', John sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands and is told to write to seven churches.
stops.watch: The letters to the churches; the throne, the four living creatures, the scroll no one can open but the Lamb 'standing as it were slain'; the seals, the horsemen, the trumpets; the woman clothed with the sun and the dragon; Babylon fallen; the rider on the white horse; the thousand years; and the last two chapters — a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down, no more death, no more night. The Bible ends where it began, with a river and a tree of life: 'Come, Lord Jesus.'
stops.after: That is the whole story. Begin it again — or turn to any stop and read it deeper.
